name: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette
role: French revolutionary, army officer and legislator
summary: Lafayette fought for American independence and proposed a declaration of rights to France’s National Assembly in 1789. He helped establish constitutional monarchy in France and pursued gradual emancipation on his estate in Cayenne.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He held military commands in America and France and introduced legislation to organize the French National Guard.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He pressed for an end to hereditary membership of the upper chamber during the revision of the Charter and again in the October 1831 debate.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: He joined the American forces fighting to end British rule and commanded troops in the campaign that forced the surrender of the British army at Yorktown.

clerical-rule.rationale: His draft allocates legislative authority to elected deputies, executive authority to the king and judicial authority to courts that apply public law.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He locates sovereignty in the nation and requires every public authority to derive expressly from it. Laws require consent through citizens or their representatives.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: At his Cayenne estate he prohibited further sales of enslaved workers, introduced wages and schooling, and set up a program aimed at gradual emancipation.

death-penalty.rationale: He called for abolition on 17 August 1830 and in October supported Victor de Tracy’s proposal to abolish capital punishment.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: His proposed declaration makes the nation the source of sovereignty and requires all public authority to flow expressly from it.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He negotiated constitutional terms for Louis-Philippe and his successors as part of the settlement that put the Orléans family on the throne.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Under the Restoration he voted against exceptional laws and opposed suspending safeguards for individual liberty.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In the Constituent Assembly he called for uniform legal standing, including civil rights for people of color, and had previously secured a measure restoring civil rights for Protestants.

harm-principle.rationale: The motion limits the exercise of natural rights only where a limit secures other people’s enjoyment of the same rights.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: He promoted the breeding of Merino sheep as part of the agricultural improvements on his estate.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: He accepted a commission in the Continental Army and fought for American independence while France was still formally at peace with Britain.

no-business-privileges.rationale: On the Franco-American commerce committee he proposed abolishing the tobacco monopoly. In 1830 he took a program opposing industrial privileges and monopolies to the Duke of Orléans.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: While a deputy under the Restoration he joined the Carbonari leadership and set out to participate in the planned Belfort uprising.

parliament-supreme.rationale: In his 16 June 1792 letter to the Legislative Assembly, Lafayette argues that the written constitution is binding on legislators and that rights limit even a constituent assembly.

party-controls-media.rationale: He opposed the Restoration ministry’s proposed censorship of newspapers in the Chamber and helped lead a society assisting people prosecuted under press restrictions.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: He joined the leadership preparing the Carbonari uprising and left for Belfort to take part before learning the plot had failed.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: His motion requires prior promulgation and lawful application of rules and calls for impartial judges.

property-fundamental.rationale: His motion lists property among rights that cannot be taken away and permits limits on natural rights only to secure their enjoyment by others.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: After the July ordinances of Charles X, he joined the revolutionary leadership and assumed command of the reconstituted National Guard.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: He joined the leaders of the Carbonari and set out to take part in their planned Belfort rising. In 1830 he assumed command of the National Guard on the side of the July Revolution.

sacred-ruler.rationale: His working draft explicitly describes the king’s person as sacred while making royal agents accountable to the nation.

second-chamber.rationale: He proposed an amendment in October 1831 to retain a chamber of peers with fifteen-year appointments and staggered renewal.

self-ownership.rationale: His motion counts complete disposal of one’s person and faculties among the inalienable rights of every person.

separated-powers.rationale: He calls for distinct legislative, executive and judicial authorities organized around free representation, official accountability and impartial judging.

shared-human-nature.rationale: His declaration grounds freedom and equality in nature and assigns inalienable rights to each person from birth.

state-harmful.rationale: He worked in the Constituent Assembly to establish ministerial responsibility and took charge of the provisional government during the July Revolution.

strong-leader.rationale: After Waterloo he secured a resolution keeping the elected Chamber permanently in session and treating any attempt to dissolve it as treason, blocking the move toward emergency dictatorship.

taxation-theft.rationale: His proposed declaration provides for public contributions with free consent and proportional apportionment.

total-state.rationale: His motion puts the exercise of natural rights beyond government control except where limits secure the same rights for others.

notes: The July 1789 motion and draft were checked against the parliamentary biography, the English memoir and correspondence, Knapp’s collection, Cornell’s Lafayette papers guide, the Cayenne exhibit and Charavay’s account and documentary appendix. Follow-up searches covered taxation and monopoly, representation and jury procedure, religion and civil rights, emancipation, the National Guard and opposition tactics, and American, Belgian and Polish independence. The reviewed record also was checked for positions on culture, ecology, technology and international institutions. Support for jury procedure does not establish a constitutional guarantee, and the Cayenne experiment does not establish compensation for descendants of enslaved people. The Seine-et-Marne archives supplied Lafayette’s comments on mechanized kneading, farm practice and the 1830 budget standoff. Those letters concern specific machinery and tax authorization. Later French memoir volumes were sought separately from the English first volume, and Charavay’s transcribed correspondence and parliamentary material provided coverage of the later period.
